title: Gut-First or Brain-First?
description: Interactive model of two competing hypotheses about Parkinson's disease. Learners choose whether misfolded alpha-synuclein starts in the gut wall or inside the brain, watch it spread along nerve connections, and compare the order of early symptoms each hypothesis predicts. A checkbox cuts the vagus nerve, which blocks gut-to-brain spread, as in a 2019 mouse study. All timings are illustrative model years.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: neuroscience (gut-brain axis)
publisher: Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk
learningObjectives: Compare the gut-first and brain-first hypotheses of Parkinson's disease by the order of early symptoms each predicts.
Explain why cutting the vagus nerve blocks spread in the gut-first route but does not change the brain-first route.
Evaluate what kind of evidence would be needed to decide between two competing hypotheses.
prerequisites: The vagus nerve connects the gut and the brainstem
Parkinson's disease involves the loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra
The difference between correlation and cause
keyQuestions: Which symptoms come before diagnosis in each proposed route?
Why does constipation years before diagnosis fit the gut-first idea, and why doesn't it prove it?
What happens to each route when the vagus nerve is cut?
What human evidence would help decide between the two hypotheses?
misconceptions: The Braak hypothesis has been proven.
Everyone with Parkinson's disease follows the same path of spread.
Constipation means a person will develop Parkinson's disease.
Cutting the vagus nerve is a way to prevent Parkinson's disease in people.
